# The cold-reader prompt, ready to paste

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). The body defines a blocking finding. Its section "The cold reader" says who reads under this prompt and what to do with what comes back.

This prompt prints every rule bound to human prose whose owner is a skill: 38 of the 63 rules the rule home carries. The rules at [`human-prose-rules.md`](human-prose-rules.md) name every other class an audit holds a text to. Judging those classes needs a rulebook the cold reader does not hold. The prompt's last instruction takes every other stop the reader met, so a class the printed list does not name still comes back.

Paste the block below verbatim into the cold-reader session, under the body's definition of a blocking finding, with the text appended.

```
You are reading a piece of text for the first time. You have no background on it: no
project history, no earlier draft, no knowledge of what the author meant beyond the words
on the page. Read it once, straight through, as a stranger who needs to understand it and
act on it.

Mark every place you stop. A stop is any one of these:
- an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning — would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
- a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists — does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?
- a name stacking two nouns with no relation between them — does this name run two nouns together, and can a reader say how the second relates to the first?
- one thing answering to a second name — does any thing named here appear under a different word somewhere else in this document or its neighbours?
- a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it — can the thing this sentence names as its subject perform this verb, or hold this quality?
- a number standing with no ground — can a reader say what this number is measured against and which way is better?
- a set pointed at by a count, a pointer, or a position, with its members never given — can a person who reads this sentence alone name the members of the set it points at?
- a text breaking a rule it states — does the sentence stating this rule obey the rule it states?
- a word grading how important or how good a thing is — does this sentence tell the reader how much to care about what it reports?
- a sentence grading the person, or grading the writer's own act — does this sentence carry a fact, or a verdict on the person's remark or on the writer's own work?
- a sentence carrying no information — does the reader do anything differently because this sentence is here?
- a word inflating a statement while adding nothing — does removing this word change what the sentence says?
- English that reads as compressed or poetic — could a native technical writer have written this sentence for an open-source project?
- the person an explanatory sentence speaks in — does this sentence tell the reader what they do, in words spoken to them?
- a sentence with no actor, or its action buried in a noun — does this sentence answer who does this, to what, and when? Does its action live in a verb?
- a judgment with no judge and no measure — who decides whether this is true, and by what measure?
- a relational word leaving its slot empty — relative to what, by what measure, or else what alternative?
- a pronoun with no antecedent in its own sentence — can a reader say which thing this pronoun points at without looking back a sentence?
- an example restating a rule that was already clear — could a reader have read this rule two ways without this example? Does this example stand in prose, outside a rule entry in the rule home?
- an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do — can the reader picture the thing this noun names?
- a paragraph carrying more than one point — does a reader who reads only the first sentences of this section still follow it?
- a reply that buries its answer — can the reader stop after the opening block and still hold the answer?
- an offer to do work the writer could already derive — does this sentence offer to do something the writer already has everything to do?
- a mistake expanded into a self-audit paragraph — does this passage explain the writer's own failure at more length than the fix takes?
- a working note handed to the reader unmarked, or a choice with no open answer — can the reader tell at a glance which lines are notes, and can they answer outside the options given?
- a task subject written in machine words — does a person glancing at this task subject know what is being done?
- one fact stated a second time in another place — does another place in this project already state this fact?
- a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them — does the entry state what the mistake is, so a writer can find an instance nobody has met yet?
- a sentence open to two readings, or hiding its cause or what it leaves out — can a reader read this sentence one way only, name what it makes happen, and say which alternatives it passed over?
- a thing named by its number, so the reader must leave the sentence to learn what it is — does this sentence say what the thing is? Does it give only a number, a position, or a count the reader must go and resolve?
- parallel items run together inside one sentence — does this sentence run several items together where a list would put one on each line?
- a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing — would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?
- a document written in the register of the message that asked for it — did this sentence take its tone from the message that asked for the work?
- a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits — does this word name the thing, or does the reader have to carry the name in from an earlier sentence?
- a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it — could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?
- a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason — does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
- a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach — can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
- a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries — reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?

For each stop, write one entry with five parts:
1. the quoted phrase;
2. where it sits (the heading or the opening words of its paragraph);
3. what a stranger cannot tell from the page alone;
4. the guess you made in place of the missing answer;
5. blocking or non-blocking.

Do not fix anything. Report only where you stopped and why. Return the entries as a numbered
list. If you stopped nowhere, say so in one line.

At every relational word, ask the three questions and write which one is unanswered: relative
to what? by what measure? or else what alternative? A word the list above does not name, that
still stopped you, is a real find — report it and note that it is new.

--- TEXT ---
<paste the text here>
```

That last instruction keeps a reader catching words the list does not carry yet. A new slot-opening word joins the weak-word list, and the skill body's weak-word lint says which copy of that list takes the edit.
